sentences.note: A command verb (imperative) addressed to a single male. The root is q-w-l ('to say'), whose middle weak letter (و) drops in the command, leaving the short form qul. There is no extra suffix: the bare form with its final silent l is itself the order 'you (one person), say'.

sentences.ar: صِرَٰطَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَنۡعَمۡتَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ غَيۡرِ ٱلۡمَغۡضُوبِ عَلَيۡهِمۡ وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ

sentences.ar: أَلَمۡ تَرَ كَيۡفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصۡحَٰبِ ٱلۡفِيلِ

in / during it (referring to the Night, feminine)

sentences.en: Nor do you worship what I worship—you have not surrendered to Allah alone as I have been commanded to do.
sentences.verseEn: Nor do you worship what I worship—you have not surrendered to Allah alone as I have been commanded to do.

words.en: worshipper / one who worships (masculine plural ending)

sentences.note: Two particles fused together. 'wa-' is the conjunction 'and', linking this verse to the one before. 'lā' is the negating particle 'not'; placed before a noun sentence here, it denies the statement as a whole. Neither word changes form for case or tense — particles are fixed.

sentences.ar: وَأَمَّا مَنۡ خَافَ مَقَامَ رَبِّهِۦ وَنَهَى ٱلنَّفۡسَ عَنِ ٱلۡهَوَىٰ

sentences.verseEn: And what will explain to you what the Night of Decree is?

words.en: made (someone) know / caused to realize you (single male)
the power / decree / measuring-out / worth (genitive ending)

sentences.note: Two pieces joined: the prefix wa- is the connector "and," linking this verse to the one before. The word mā here is an interrogative, "what," used not for real inquiry but rhetorically to stress the greatness of what follows. It has no case ending of its own; it stands as the subject of the question.

sentences.en: We sent it—the Qur'an—down on the Night of Decree, Laylat al-Qadr—
sentences.verseEn: We sent it—the Qur'an—down on the Night of Decree, Laylat al-Qadr—

words.en: indeed / truly (strong emphasis) we (attached pronoun, the divine 'We')
sent down / caused to descend (Form IV) we (subject: Allah, majestic plural) it / him (object: the Qur'an)
the (definite article) power / decree / measuring-out / high worth

sentences.note: 'Inna' is an emphasis-particle placed at the head of a sentence to assert it firmly; render it as 'indeed' or 'most certainly'. The attached '-nā' is the pronoun 'we', referring to Allah in the majestic plural — not a literal numerical plural but a marker of supreme greatness.…

sentences.en: I will never worship what you worship—no social pressure, no compromise for peace at the price of shirk, will change that.
sentences.verseEn: I will never worship what you worship—no social pressure, no compromise for peace at the price of shirk, will change that.

words.en: worshipper / one who worships a (indefinite marker)
what / that which (here: the act of)

sentences.note: Two particles fused into one word. The prefix wa- means "and" and ties this verse to the one before it. lā is the negation "not"; here it negates the noun-based (nominal) sentence that follows ("I am not a worshipper of..."), giving an absolute, ongoing denial rather than a one-time "I did not."

sentences.en: And from the evil of darkness when it settles—literal night and the inner night of despair, rumination, and the thoughts that grow when you are alone with your screen or your fears.
sentences.verseEn: And from the evil of darkness when it settles—literal night and the inner night of despair, rumination, and the thoughts that grow when you are alone with your screen or your fears.
sentences.note: Two pieces joined together. The wa- is a connector meaning 'and', tying this verse to the request for refuge in the verse before. min is a preposition meaning 'from', marking the source or origin of the evil. A preposition like min puts the noun after it into the genitive case, which is why the next word ends in -i.

sentences.en: And from the evil of those who blow on knots—those who secretly work harm through envy, manipulation, or hidden schemes meant to undo your peace.
sentences.verseEn: And from the evil of those who blow on knots—those who secretly work harm through envy, manipulation, or hidden schemes meant to undo your peace.

words.en: the women who blow much/repeatedly (of) — genitive ending

sentences.note: Two joined particles. The wa- prefix is a connector meaning 'and', tying this phrase to the earlier 'I seek refuge ... from ...'. 'min' is a preposition meaning 'from', and it forces the noun after it (sharri) into the genitive case, which is why that next word ends in -i.…

sentences.en: And from the evil of an envier when he envies—when someone resents your blessings, your stability, or your faith and wishes them gone.
sentences.verseEn: And from the evil of an envier when he envies—when someone resents your blessings, your stability, or your faith and wishes them gone.
sentences.note: Written as one word in the text (wamin) but built from two pieces. "wa-" is the connector "and," tying this verse to the earlier ones. "min" is a preposition meaning "from"; here it marks the source of evil one takes refuge against.…

sentences.ar: إِنَّآ أَنذَرۡنَٰكُمۡ عَذَابٗا قَرِيبٗا يَوۡمَ يَنظُرُ ٱلۡمَرۡءُ مَا قَدَّمَتۡ يَدَاهُ وَيَقُولُ ٱلۡكَافِرُ يَٰلَيۡتَنِي كُنتُ تُرَٰبَۢا
sentences.en: Indeed, We have warned you of an imminent punishment—the Day every person will see ˹the consequences of˺ what their hands have done, and the disbelievers will cry, “I wish I were dust.”
sentences.tr: innā andharnākum ʿadhāban qarīban yawma yanẓuru l-maru mā qaddamat yadāhu wayaqūlu l-kāfiru yālaytanī kuntu turāban

sentences.ar: لَّهُۥ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِۗ
sentences.en: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.
sentences.verseEn: Allah — there is no god worthy of worship except Him, the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth. Who can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they grasp none of His knowledge except what He wills. His Kursi — the Footstool symbolizing His dominion over creation — encompasses the heavens and earth, and their preservation does not weary Him. He is the Most High, the Greatest.
sentences.tr: la-hu mā fī al-samāwāt--i wa-mā fī al--arḍ--i
sentences.note: A preposition 'li-' ('to/for') fused with the attached pronoun 'him'. The pronoun 'him' stays the same; it is the preposition that changes, its vowel shifting from -i (li-) to -a (la-) when an attached pronoun follows it directly. The whole unit commonly conveys possession or that something is for someone's benefit.

sentences.en: And guarding them both does not weary Him.
sentences.verseEn: Allah — there is no god worthy of worship except Him, the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. words.en: he / it (does) weary / burden indicative ending (-u) him
guarding / preserving nominative ending (-u) the two of them / both of them

sentences.note: 'wa' is 'and'. 'lā' is a negating particle; placed before a verb of command it expresses prohibition ('do not ...'), and before other verbs/nouns it expresses negation ('not ...'). It carries no case ending.

sentences.en: He has no fear of consequences.
and bind ˹them˺ tightly, like no other.

sentences.note: This is a non-inflecting preposition (it never changes its ending). It governs the noun after it and forces that noun into the genitive case — which is why the next word 'sharr' takes an -i ending (sharri). Think of it as 'from' pulling whatever follows into a 'from-the-X' relationship.

sentences.en: You have blessed THEM. (1:7)
sentences.note: Arabic attaches its pronouns to the END of words: ـِي my (رَبِّي my Lord), ـكَ your (رَبُّكَ your Lord), ـهُ his/him (لَهُ to him), ـهُمْ their/them (عَلَيْهِمْ upon them), ـنَا our/us (اهْدِنَا guide us). Master these five endings and huge amounts of Quran unlock.
sentences.theme: attached pronouns — my, your, his, their

sentences.note: This is the prefix particle wa- ("and"), used to connect clauses. It carries no case ending of its own; it simply attaches to whatever follows and ties this line to the one before it. In the running verse it pairs with the negative that follows to give "and not / nor."

sentences.ar: لَّا يَذُوقُونَ فِيهَا بَرۡدٗا وَلَا شَرَابًا

sentences.en: We have given you, O Prophet, al-Kawthar—abundant good in this life and the next: honour, a lasting legacy, intercession, and a river in Paradise that those who mocked you will never reach.

sentences.note: Inna is an emphasising particle that opens the sentence and makes its claim sound certain and weighty ('it is truly the case that...'). The attached ending -nā is the pronoun 'we', referring to Allah in the royal/majestic plural (a plural of greatness, not of number).…

sentences.en: You are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺.
It will be sealed over them,

sentences.note: إِنَّ starts a sentence with force: 'indeed / truly'. It's everywhere in the Quran. Practical rule: after إِنَّ the noun takes -a (accusative): إِنَّ اللهَ، إِنَّ الإِنسَانَ. With pronouns it fuses: إِنَّهُ (indeed he), إِنَّا (indeed we), إِنَّكَ (indeed you).

words.en: you (do) worship / serve (masculine plural) you all

sentences.en: That knowledge rests with your Lord ˹alone˺.
˹For˺ your Lord is truly vigilant.

sentences.en: In the flat there are two big rooms — the adjective goes dual as well.
sentences.note:
English has one and many. Arabic has one, TWO, and many — and the two is an ENDING, not a word. You never say the number.

MAKING IT, in one step: add ـَانِ to the singular. خَال → خَالَانِ (two uncles), كِتَاب → كِتَابَانِ (two books). If the word ends in ة, the ة opens up into ت first: خَالَة → خَالَتَانِ, غُرْفَة → غُرْفَتَانِ. That is the whole rule she was giving you.

THE SECOND ENDING, which is where it usually confuses people: ـَانِ is only for the DOER of the sentence. Everywhere else — after a preposition, or as the thing being acted on — it becomes ـَيْنِ. خَالَانِ فِي البَيْتِ (two uncles are in the house) but مَعَ خَالَيْنِ (with two uncles). Say them out loud — ‘-aan’ and ‘-ayn’ — and you will hear which one a sentence wants.

Anything describing a dual goes dual too: غُرْفَتَانِ كَبِيرَتَانِ, two big rooms. And a few words are almost always dual: وَالِدَانِ (parents), يَدَانِ (hands), عَيْنَانِ (eyes). From the class of 30 Aug.

sentences.en: I went with two uncles — after مَعَ it must be ـَيْنِ, not ـَانِ.
sentences.note:
English has one and many. Arabic has one, TWO, and many — and the two is an ENDING, not a word. You never say the number.

MAKING IT, in one step: add ـَانِ to the singular. خَال → خَالَانِ (two uncles), كِتَاب → كِتَابَانِ (two books). If the word ends in ة, the ة opens up into ت first: خَالَة → خَالَتَانِ, غُرْفَة → غُرْفَتَانِ. That is the whole rule she was giving you.

Everywhere else — after a preposition, or as the thing being acted on — it becomes ـَيْنِ. خَالَانِ فِي البَيْتِ (two uncles are in the house) but مَعَ خَالَيْنِ (with two uncles). Say them out loud — ‘-aan’ and ‘-ayn’ — and you will hear which one a sentence wants.

sentences.en: There is no lift.
sentences.note: To say something exists somewhere, Arabic uses يُوجَدُ ('is found'), or just puts the place first with no verb at all: فِي المَطْبَخِ ثَلَّاجَةٌ — 'in the kitchen (is) a fridge'. There is no word for 'is'. The question form is the one she put on the board: مَاذَا يُوجَدُ فِي بَيْتِكَ؟
